summary: Adds support for salted password databases to EAP-pwd, an authentication method that uses a shared password and resists dictionary attacks. Many existing credential stores keep salted passwords, and the base method did not handle them. It updates RFC 5931.

eli5.summary: Some websites mix a pinch of random spice into stored passwords. This lets a login method work with those spiced passwords.

questions: how does eap-pwd use salted passwords
what is a salt in password storage
which hash functions does eap-pwd support for salting
subtitle: How EAP-pwd can authenticate against password databases that store salted hashes instead of plain passwords.

tldr.problem: EAP-pwd needs both sides to hold an identical processed form of the password, but many existing databases store only salted passwords, which the base method could not use.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines new password preprocessing techniques (salted SHA-1, SHA-256 and SHA-512, UNIX crypt, scrypt and PBKDF2) and adds a salt length and salt to the EAP-pwd-Commit/Request message.
tldr.outcome: Deployed salted databases can be used with EAP-pwd, but the salted password acts as the credential, so the database must be protected like a plaintext password database.

today: RFC 8146 is an Informational RFC that updates RFC 5931; it has not been obsoleted or updated by a later RFC.

sections.title: Why Salted Passwords Matter
sections.content:
A stolen password database reveals passwords. To make that harder, a random salt is hashed with the password and the digest is stored with the salt. Two users with the same password then have different stored values, and an attacker must run a dictionary attack per entry.

The RFC says salting alone is not enough against dictionary attacks, especially with custom hardware, and that a sequential memory hard function such as the one in RFC 7914 should be used. Still, many salted databases are deployed, and EAP-pwd needs to support them as well as databases using more modern functions.
sections.eli5: Salt is a pinch of random spice mixed into every password, so even two identical passwords look different once stored.

sections.title: Password Preprocessing Techniques
sections.content:
EAP-pwd is based on the dragonfly password-authenticated key exchange (RFC 7664), a balanced exchange where each party must obtain an identical processed password. Salting is therefore treated as extra password preprocessing. The server tells the peer which salt and digest to use.

The RFC defines new techniques, identified by codes 0x03 to 0x10: a random salt with SHA-1, SHA-256 or SHA-512; UNIX crypt(); scrypt; PBKDF2 with SHA-256 or SHA-512; and variants that first apply SASLprep or OpaqueString. Plain salting is included for existing databases, while scrypt and PBKDF2 are RECOMMENDED for new deployments.

The salt SHOULD be at least as long as the digest of the hash used, but a peer SHOULD NOT abort just because a deployed database used a shorter salt.
sections.eli5: There is a menu of recipes for mixing the spice into the password. Both sides must pick the same recipe so they end up with the same result.

sections.title: Salting, crypt, scrypt and PBKDF2
sections.content:
For plain salting, the password is hashed followed by the salt: salted-password = Hash(password | salt). The server stores the salted password and salt, and the client derives the salted password on the fly.

With crypt(), the whole salt, including the encoded setting that selects the algorithm, is passed as an opaque string. If the client does not support the algorithm the server indicates, the exchange fails and the client MUST terminate the connection.

For scrypt, the parameters N, r, p and dkLen are packed into the salt field as N || r || p || dkLen || salt. The values r and dkLen are 16-bit integers and the others are 32-bit, all in network order. For PBKDF2, the iteration count c and dkLen are 16-bit integers: c || dkLen || salt.
sections.eli5: Each recipe has its own settings, like how long to stir. Those settings travel along with the spice so the other side can follow the same steps.

sections.title: Changes to the EAP-pwd Exchange
sections.content:
The server proposes a preprocessing technique in EAP-pwd-ID/Request, before it knows who the client is. This means one password database can use only one salt digest; supporting several needs several databases, selected by the routable part of the client identity. The client accepts a technique in EAP-pwd-ID/Response, or terminates if it accepts none.

Once the server knows the identity, it looks up the salted password and salt and adds the salt length and salt to the EAP-pwd-Commit/Request. The client's Commit/Response is unchanged and MUST NOT echo the salt. The salt length SHALL be non-zero, and the Element and Scalar are encoded as in RFC 5931. For non-salted methods the Commit payload MUST NOT include the salt.
sections.eli5: The server says which recipe to use, then hands over the spice jar's label along with its next message. The client does not need to send it back.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Because both sides must produce an identical processed password, a salted password stolen from a database can be used directly to impersonate the EAP-pwd client, with no dictionary attack needed. The per-user salt still keeps the adversary from recovering the original password for other uses. Salted databases used with EAP-pwd MUST be protected as well as plaintext password databases.

EAP-pwd sends the salt in the clear. Unless it is tunneled in an encrypting EAP method, an observer can learn the salt for a user, which is extra metadata but does not by itself reveal the password.
sections.eli5: If a thief steals the spiced passwords, they can pretend to be users on this system, so the jar must be guarded as carefully as the real passwords.
